label: Three Examples of Coupling Techniques
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 21 through 28 and treats coupling not as a definition to memorize but as a working proof method. Three small models show the same trick: replace a hard comparison of two laws by an easy pointwise estimate on a cleverly chosen joint law.

label: What Is a Coupling
notes: A coupling of two probability measures is any joint law whose two marginals recover them. Couplings always exist, since the product measure is one, and the freedom in choosing the joint law is exactly the leverage every argument in this chapter exploits to its advantage.

label: Coupling as a Proof Method
notes: The recurring move is to push the difficulty into the construction of a joint law and then read off a bound pointwise. A pathwise or coordinatewise inequality, once integrated against the coupling, becomes a statement about the two original distributions for free.

label: The Monotone Coupling on the Line
notes: On the real line the optimal coupling is explicit: match equal quantiles. The increasing rearrangement sends the p-th quantile of mu to the p-th quantile of nu, giving a nondecreasing transport map. This deterministic coupling is optimal for every convex cost simultaneously.

label: Rearrangement and Correlation Inequalities
notes: Coupling two variables through their shared quantile makes them comonotone, so any supermodular score is maximized. This single construction yields Hardy-Littlewood rearrangement bounds and Chebyshev's correlation inequality, each becoming a pointwise comparison after the increasing matching is fixed.

label: Synchronous Langevin Coupling
notes: Run two diffusions from different starts but drive them with one shared Brownian motion. Under convexity of the potential the gap between the trajectories contracts deterministically, so shared noise converts an analytic spectral-gap question into a visible pathwise shrinking distance.

label: From Pathwise Control to Wasserstein
notes: The coupled trajectories give a candidate joint law of the two time-t distributions, so their Wasserstein distance is bounded by the expected pathwise gap. A coordinate inequality holding almost surely upgrades immediately to exponential convergence of the laws to equilibrium.

label: Knothe-Rosenblatt Triangular Maps
notes: When no canonical order exists in higher dimension, build a map one coordinate at a time. Each conditional is matched by its own increasing rearrangement, producing a triangular map with nonnegative Jacobian whose structure makes determinant and trace estimates tractable.

label: A Transport Route to Isoperimetry
notes: Transport a reference body onto a competitor and track the Jacobian of the triangular map. The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality applied to its eigenvalues turns the volume constraint into a surface bound, recovering the isoperimetric inequality from a pointwise change-of-variables estimate.

label: Choosing the Right Coupling
notes: The three examples differ only in which joint law is clever. Monotone matching exploits order, synchronous noise exploits convex drift, triangular maps exploit conditioning. In every case the verification collapses to one inequality evaluated pointwise and then averaged against the coupling.

label: Computational Footprint
notes: The companion notebook rebuilds the chapter as a finite Monge-Kantorovich plan whose rows and columns must equal the prescribed marginals. A contraction-mode figure plus a JSON invariant check confirm mass conservation, making the coupling argument inspectable rather than merely asserted.

label: Summary and Takeaways
notes: Coupling is a unifier: contraction, comparison, and transport-based inequality are three faces of the same method. Build a joint law that makes the inequality obvious pointwise, integrate, and a hard distributional comparison dissolves into elementary bookkeeping checked by the marginals.
